verdict.reasoning: Patient states: “Over the past few days, I've noticed my skin is sore and red” and later confirms it is “very itchy and dry.”
Location described as: “It's all over my chest, my hands and arms, especially inside of the elbows.” The antecubital fossae correspond to the inside of the elbows.
When asked if this is similar or worse, patient replies: “I think it's gotten worse. Like this past few… days.” indicating the current flare is worse than previous eczema.
When asked about weeping: “Is it weeping? ...” patient replies: “No.”
Clinician asks about thickened, darkened skin: “Is there any thickened skin...?” Patient responds: “No. No, I don't think so.” Lichenification corresponds to thickened skin.
On scratch marks: “Any scratch marks?” Patient answers: “There's no scratch mark.”
Clinician asks: “Otherwise... you're feeling well... there's no temperature...?” Patient does not report fever, implying denial of temperature/fever.
Same question: “there's no temperature, no joint pains?” Patient replies affirmatively to feeling well; later confirms “yeah, no joint pain.”
Clinician: “Otherwise, other than those rash, you're feeling well in yourself...?” Context and lack of other complaints support that patient feels otherwise well.
Patient: “Yes, I have Eczema in the past.”
Patient: “I have asthma...”
Patient: “Usually I use a cream called Dipro Base.”
Patient: “In the shower I use something called Dermal.”
Patient confirms using hydrocortisone: “Yeah. So you're using the hydrocortisone? Yeah.” and earlier: “Yes, you used it, but it. It's not helping.” indicating minimal effect.
Regarding asthma meds: patient uses “the blue inhaler” and agrees they use it “on and off,” i.e., as needed.

Patient: “I realized I've tried also antihistamines and didn't work.” Asked which one: “The one over the counter.” Clinician: “Okay, so like cetrazene? Yeah, yeah, yeah.” indicating OTC cetirizine, ineffective.
Clinician: “Do you have any allergies to any medication at all?” Patient: “No, no allergies.”
Patient: “My mother has migraine.”
On family history: “in my family there is hypothyroidism and migraine. My mother has migraine.” Clarified: “Who has hypothyroidism? ... My mother.”

Clinician: “it looks like… it is quite widespread, your eczema” and later notes need for stronger steroid because current hydrocortisone and prior antihistamines “didn't work,” while patient has been using emollients consistently; this supports extensive, worsening, and refractory eczema.
For asthma: “you don't use it every day. So you just use it on and off? Yeah, yeah, yeah.” This aligns with intermittent asthma with as-needed inhaler use.
Clinician: “you would probably need some antihistamines which I'm going to prescribe… it's called the antihistamine it's called fexofenadine.”

Clinician: “You might probably need a bit more stronger one like betno weight or something like that. Okay, so we'll try that first.” and “use it twice a day for the next couple of weeks” with fingertip unit explanation. Betamethasone valerate 0.1% strength is not specified in the transcript.
Clinician: “You still need to continue on your emollients like the dermal soap and as well as the depravate [Diprobase].”
The plan regarding asthma or blue inhaler use is not discussed in the plan section; only current usage is described. No explicit instruction to use the blue inhaler as needed is given as a new plan.
Clinician: “we are going to send off the prescription to your pharmacy. It looks like Boots on the systems… So I'll send it across to Boots and it will be there for collecting.”

Clinician: “If there's no improvement, you need to get back to us. Or if you have any kind of adverse reaction... you need to get in touch with us… If things are getting worse in the next two weeks, call us beforehand. Otherwise, wait for two weeks...”
